ethics_check.title: Ethics Approval Check
ethics_check.summary_text: 1 of 1 paper appeared to involve live data collection and lacked an ethics approval statement.

table.text: We recruited 200 participants through Prolific (50% female, 42% White, 36 years old on average).
Procedure Participants were given some examples of asymmetries of analogical directions (outside of the base and target domains).
Thus, we recruited 300 total participants on Prolific (50% female, 46% White, 36 years on average).
After a brief introduction to the task (slightly varied from Study 1 to ensure robustness), participants were given 6 comparison trials and 6 filler trials.
Participants were simply asked which analogy was better on a 7-point Likert scale.
After completing all 12 trials and an attention check, participants were thanked for their time and compensated.
Thus, we recruited 200 participants on Prolific (50% female, 46% White, 36 years on average).
Participants were given a refresher of what an analogy is, and an example (the Bohr model of the atom).
Given our design, this required the recruitment of 300 total participants on Prolific (50% female, 52% White, 37 years on average).
Participants were given 6 comparison trials and 6 filler trials, where they were asked which analogy was better on a 7-point Likert scale.
After completing all 12 trials (which were randomized), and an attention check, participants were thanked for their time and compensated.

We observed this asymmetry when comparing the best analogies in either direction (Study 1), when we randomly paired bases and targets in either direction (Study 2), and when participants were asked to generate their own analogies (Study 3).
Finally, our participants were recruited largely from wealthy, English speaking nations.

report: Reporting *p* values imprecisely (e.g., *p* < .05) reduces transparency, reproducibility, and re-use (e.g., in *p* value meta-analyses). Best practice is to report exact p-values with three decimal places (e.g., *p* = .032) unless *p* values are smaller than 0.001, in which case you can use *p* < .001.

This module sometimes flags false positives when sentences discuss how p-value thresholds were set. It can also miss an imprecise p-value that is reported against a threshold (e.g., "decreased at the *p* < .05 significance threshold").

```{r}
#| echo: false


# table data --------------------------------------
table <- structure(list("P-Value" = "p's > 0.07", Text = "There was no difference between analogies with the physical mechanical base in length and word frequency compared to the other domains (p's > 0.07) and as before, including length and frequency as covariates for the analogies did not change the significance of any effects."), row.names = c(NA, 
-1L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame"))

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 2, FALSE)
```

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} The APA manual states: Report exact *p* values (e.g., *p* = .031) to two or three decimal places. However, report *p* values less than .001 as *p* < .001. However, 2 decimals is too imprecise for many use-cases (e.g., a *p* value meta-analysis), so report *p* values with three digits. American Psychological Association (2020). Publication manual of the American Psychological Association, 7 edition. American Psychological Association. :::

stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. #### Code Comments
Best programming practice is to add comments to code, to explain what the code does (to yourself in the future, or peers who want to re-use your code).
#### Missing Files
All files loaded in the code were present in the repository.
#### Absolute Paths

Best programming practice is to use relative file paths (e.g., './files') instead of absolute file paths (e.g., 'C://Lakens/project_dir/files') as these folder names do not exist on other computers. No absolute file paths were found in any of the code files.
#### Working Directory (setwd)

Best programming practice is to avoid `setwd()` in analysis code: it hardcodes an assumption about the working directory (often an absolute path on the author's own machine), so the code breaks when run anywhere else. Keep the working directory as the caller sets it and use relative paths. No `setwd()` calls were found in any of the code files.
#### Package Installation (install.packages)

Best programming practice is to avoid `install.packages()` in analysis code: it installs software on whoever runs the script without asking, which is at minimum disruptive (an unexpected install, network access, a package version the author never tested against) and at worst a security risk if it points at an untrusted repository. Document required packages instead (a README, or a list of them: an `renv.lock`/`DESCRIPTION` for R, a `requirements.txt` for Python). No `install.packages()` calls were found in any of the code files.
#### Libraries / Imports
Best programming practice is to load all required libraries/imports in one block near the top of the code. In all code files, libraries/imports were loaded in one block.
#### Packages / Dependencies

The code files load 10 distinct packages/libraries: broom.mixed, emmeans, LexOPS, lmerTest, patchwork, ragg, stringi, systemfonts, tidytext, tidyverse. These are the names found in the source (no version information is available from static analysis).
#### Reproducible Environment

No `renv.lock` file, `sessionInfo()`/`session_info()` record, or `groundhog`/`checkpoint` date-pin call was found anywhere in the repository. Without one of these, the exact R and package versions used for the analysis are not recoverable, and package versions may drift between when this analysis was run and any later reproduction attempt. :::

This module runs automated data-quality checks (empty columns, SPSS filter variables, category casing, stray whitespace, numbers stored as text, problematic and colliding column names, mixed text encodings, personal information, spreadsheet formatting, and careless responding) on the extracted data files.
We examined 541 columns across 24 data files.
#### Issues Identified

65 file/column combinations have at least one issue.

**About the personal-information flags.** These are pattern matches, not confirmed disclosures, and they are tuned to over-report rather than miss something. Expect false positives:

- **Column names** are matched against identifying words in English and other European languages (`email`, `telefoonnummer`, `geboortedatum`, ...). A column called `phone_number` flags whether or not it holds one, and an empty or already-anonymised column flags on its name alone.
- **Values** are matched against the shape of an identifier. An IP address pattern also matches a version string or a dotted numeric code; a card-number pattern requires both a real issuer prefix and a checksum, but a long numeric ID can still coincide.
- **Free text** is flagged when a column holds long, mostly-distinct prose — the shape open-ended answers take. Most such columns contain no names at all.

A flag means *look at this column*. Where the data is already de-identified (an `ip` column reading `Anonymized`, a `name` column the authors emptied), no action is needed.

#### Careless Responding
No file could be screened for careless responding.

**What this does not cover.** Only 0 of 24 data files could be screened: the rest had no detectable multi-item scale block, or too few respondents. Even in a screened file, these checks only look at multi-item rating scales — the only place where a repeated or flat answer pattern is interpretable. Single questions, open text, demographics and any item outside a detected scale block are never examined. A respondent can therefore answer most of a survey carelessly and still not be flagged here, and finding nothing is not evidence that a dataset is free of careless responding.

reproducibility_check.summary_text:
-  We assessed AND ran 14 R code files for reproducibility (each in an isolated Docker container).
-  10 of 13 scripts ran without error when executed (1 more is run by another script with `source()`).
-  3 scripts could not run because their own dependency is unavailable (not counted against the traffic light).
-  10 installable dependencies detected.
- 193 statistics stored from the extracted output; 2 of 39 reported tests matched (5.1%).

live_data_statements: We recruited 200 participants through Prolific (50% female, 42% White, 36 years old on average).
Procedure Participants were given some examples of asymmetries of analogical directions (outside of the base and target domains).
Thus, we recruited 300 total participants on Prolific (50% female, 46% White, 36 years on average).
After a brief introduction to the task (slightly varied from Study 1 to ensure robustness), participants were given 6 comparison trials and 6 filler trials.
Participants were simply asked which analogy was better on a 7-point Likert scale.
After completing all 12 trials and an attention check, participants were thanked for their time and compensated.
Thus, we recruited 200 participants on Prolific (50% female, 46% White, 36 years on average).
Participants were given a refresher of what an analogy is, and an example (the Bohr model of the atom).
Given our design, this required the recruitment of 300 total participants on Prolific (50% female, 52% White, 37 years on average).
Participants were given 6 comparison trials and 6 filler trials, where they were asked which analogy was better on a 7-point Likert scale.
After completing all 12 trials (which were randomized), and an attention check, participants were thanked for their time and compensated.

We observed this asymmetry when comparing the best analogies in either direction (Study 1), when we randomly paired bases and targets in either direction (Study 2), and when participants were asked to generate their own analogies (Study 3).
Finally, our participants were recruited largely from wealthy, English speaking nations.

#### File paths

#### Execution
**The code was run.** Each script ran in an isolated Docker container against a throwaway copy of the repository, in the run order above, with a 300-second per-script timeout. Of 14 scripts: 10 ran without error, 0 errored, 0 timed out, 3 could not run because one of its own dependencies is unavailable, 0 did not parse, and 1 was run by another script with `source()`. Running against current package versions: a break can reflect version drift, which argues for pinning versions.

**Dependency-unavailable errors**
**3 scripts could not run because their own dependency is unavailable** — the package failed to install from both live CRAN and the CRAN Archive (or a GitHub/URL source could not be resolved). This is an infrastructure limitation, not a defect in the paper's code, so it does **not** force the traffic light red.

1 script is run by another script with `source()`, so it was not run on its own: each script runs in a fresh R process, and on its own a sourced script lacks the packages and objects the sourcing script sets up first. Its outcome is part of the sourcing script's outcome.

info.title: MECHANICAL AND PSYCHOLOGICAL DOMAINS OF THOUGHT ARE ANALOGICALLY ASYMMETRICAL

text.text: Psychology and physics are two core domains of human cognition.
Little is known about their epistemic relation.
Does our understanding of common physical-mechanical systems better inform our understanding of psychology, or vice versa?
To answer this question, we compared analogies that explain one domain in terms of the other.
In Study 1, we found the best analogies with a mechanical base explaining a psychological target were preferred to the best analogies in the opposite direction.
In Study 2, we generated analogies from random pairings of mechanical and psychological systems and again found a preference for analogies with a mechanical base.
In Study 3, participants overwhelmingly generated analogies with a mechanical (instead of psychological) base.
And Study 4 showed that analogies with a mechanical base were also preferred to those with bases from other domains.
These results suggest that the physical-mechanical domain may serve as a privileged launchpad for explanation.
These studies find that participants generally prefer cases where physical-mechanical systems are used to explain psychological systems, as well as chemical, biological, and economic phenomena.
Thus, physical-mechanical systems (in particular, artifacts) may serve as fertile ground for explanation.
In contrast to prior work, which has examined the relations between individual analogies, these studies illustrate asymmetries between analogies at the level of large-scale domain.
Discoveries and explanations in the sciences often progress through analogies (e.g., Lombrozo, 2024; Thagard, 2021).
text.formatted: Discoveries and explanations in the sciences often progress through analogies (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">Lombrozo, 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">Thagard, 2021)</ref>.

text.text: Causal relational patterns are identified in a base and transferred to a target.
Orbital patterns in the solar system (base) are transferred to the atom (target); the relations between a lock and a key are transferred to those between an enzyme and its substrate.
The utility of such analogies is typically asymmetrical; only rarely does swapping target and base yield comparably useful insights.
The base presumably has more information for understanding the target than the opposite.

While extensive research has examined individual analogies (Gentner et al., 2001; Gentner, 2025), including asymmetrical cases (Bowdle & Gentner, 1997; Bassok & Holyoak, 1989; Mo & Gentner, 2024), a central question remains: are large domains analogically asymmetrical with other large domains?
text.formatted: While extensive research has examined individual analogies <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(Gentner et al., 2001;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">Gentner, 2025)</ref>, including asymmetrical cases <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Bowdle & Gentner, 1997;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">Bassok & Holyoak, 1989;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">Mo & Gentner, 2024)</ref>, a central question remains: are large domains analogically asymmetrical with other large domains?

text.text: Here, we examine versions of two of the most early emerging and universal domains of human knowledge: physical/mechanical and psychological entities.

Analogical asymmetries have previously been assumed to arise from idiosyncrasies of specific base target combinations (where a base has a particular set of relations that inform the target which has far fewer such relations to provide in return).

Here, we propose that the majority of all possible bases and targets between the mechanical and psychological domains pattern in the same way: physical bases should be more informative than psychological ones.

Intuitive physical mechanics and psychology are widely seen as two fundamental domains of early emerging knowledge in humans (e.g., Carey & Spelke, 1996; Gopnik & Wellman, 2012), and of ontology in philosophy (Descartes, 1641 (Descartes, /2016;; Strawson, 1959; Carruthers, 2002).
text.formatted: Intuitive physical mechanics and psychology are widely seen as two fundamental domains of early emerging knowledge in humans (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">Carey & Spelke, 1996;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">Gopnik & Wellman, 2012)</ref>, and of ontology in philosophy <ref type="bibr">(Descartes, 1641</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(Descartes, /2016;;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">Strawson, 1959;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">Carruthers, 2002)</ref>.

text.text: They constitute vast swaths of what we know and guide further knowledge growth.
Their (in)ability to analogically inform each other should reveal how such foundational domains interact in exploration and discovery.
We speculate that physical mechanical systems are the more potent analogical launch pads.
This is for several reasons.
Mechanical systems often have nested stable subassemblies with distinct causal roles (Simon,1996).
text.formatted: Mechanical systems often have nested stable subassemblies with distinct causal roles <ref type="bibr">(Simon,1996)</ref>.

text.text: Mechanical parts amplify forces (e.g., levers), store energy (e.g., springs), and join elements (e.g., nuts and bolts).
Different combinations of a small number of such components can constitute an unlimited number of unique but comprehensible devices.
Because their causal relations are usually easy to interpret in spatial terms, they may be easier to remember and mentally manipulate (Bellmund et al., 2018).
text.formatted: Because their causal relations are usually easy to interpret in spatial terms, they may be easier to remember and mentally manipulate <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(Bellmund et al., 2018)</ref>.

text.text: Evidence that physical mechanical systems provide more powerful analogical bases would be especially striking given intuitive psychology's dominance in everyday conversations.
Psychological phenomena are discussed more frequently (e.g., Dunbar, Marriott, & Duncan, 1997), with some estimates approaching 90% of natural conversations (Schmeichel, et al, 2025).
text.formatted: Psychological phenomena are discussed more frequently (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">Dunbar, Marriott, & Duncan, 1997)</ref>, with some estimates approaching 90% of natural conversations <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">(Schmeichel, et al, 2025)</ref>.

text.text: In addition, many of the metaphors used in daily speech apply psychological notions to other realms (Lakoff & Johnson, 2008).
text.formatted: In addition, many of the metaphors used in daily speech apply psychological notions to other realms <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">(Lakoff & Johnson, 2008)</ref>.

text.text: But such cases (such as cars whining, growling and purring), usually involve transferring a descriptive property to the other category, not a causal explanation.
While greater familiarity may make humans more fluent in psychological discourse and may support powerful behavioral predictions, it may not enable effective analogical bases for other large domains.
More generally, simply having a vast amount of knowledge and experience in a domain is not enough to make it a productive base for analogies.
The nature of the knowledge is critical.

To explore a favored status for mechanical over psychological systems in analogies, we compared what Large Language Models (LLMs) generate as typical analogies of mechanics informing psychology and the reverse.

LLMs are built out of large text corpora that include many analogies (Webb, Holyoak, & Lu, 2023; Larraz & Corma, 2026); and if those text collections show asymmetries in the quality of analogies generated, those asymmetries are likely to represent natural human tendencies.
text.formatted: LLMs are built out of large text corpora that include many analogies <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">(Webb, Holyoak, & Lu, 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">Larraz & Corma, 2026)</ref>; and if those text collections show asymmetries in the quality of analogies generated, those asymmetries are likely to represent natural human tendencies.

text.text: Study 1 compared human judgments of LLM generated best analogies in either direction.
Study 2 compared judgments of analogies generated from randomly generated pairings in either direction.
Study 3 tested these results without the use of LLMs by having participants create novel analogies in both directions.
Finally, Study 4 asked whether asymmetries favoring the mechanical might extend beyond psychology.

In this study, we asked participants whether some of the best analogies explaining a physical mechanical phenomenon in terms of the psychological were better than some of the best analogies explaining a psychological phenomenon in terms of the physical mechanical.
Because this was meant to be a comparison between sets of analogies whose quality should be at ceiling, it represents a conservative test of the proposed analogical asymmetry hypothesis.

text.formatted: Code and stimuli are available at GitHub: <ref type="url" target="https://github.com/martxgr/analogies">https://github.com/martxgr/analogies</ref> Participants Power analyses from pilot data suggested 200 participants would give us over 80% power for our analyses.

text.text: We recruited 200 participants through Prolific (50% female, 42% White, 36 years old on average).
Participants who failed our one preregistered attention check were excluded from the analysis (n = 6).
Stimuli were generated using ChatGPT (5.6 Sol).

First, we prompted it (without access to memory, so as to eliminate any influence prior chats): "Give me the 6 best analogies in which a purely physical-mechanical system is explained in terms of a purely psychological system.
Please write each analogy in the form "x is like y:" and keep it to 2 sentences."
Next, we prompted it (again without access to memory): "Give me the 6 best analogies in which a purely psychological system is explained in terms of a purely physical-mechanical system.
Please write each analogy in the form "x is like y:" and keep it to 2 sentences."
The same procedure was performed using biological and economic systems to provide filler analogies in order to reduce the salience of the contrast of interest.
Then, we randomly selected 3 pairings of the physical-mechanical and psychological analogies, and 3 pairings for biological and economic systems to construct a "block".
We generated 6 blocks, such that whether the analogy with the mechanical or psychological base came first in the pairing was counterbalanced across subjects.
Below is an example of a pairing: [mechanism base] Attention is like a movable spotlight: it illuminates a narrow region of a larger field, making whatever falls inside it easier to inspect.
Moving the beam toward one target necessarily leaves other targets in relative darkness.
[psychological base] A spring is like expectation under tension: the farther reality is displaced from what is expected, the stronger the psychological pressure to restore consistency.
Likewise, stretching or compressing a spring creates a restoring force that increases with displacement.
Procedure Participants were given some examples of asymmetries of analogical directions (outside of the base and target domains).

Then, they were then shown pairings of one of the best analogies where a psychological phenomenon was explained by a physical-mechanical one and where a physical-mechanical phenomenon was explained by a psychological one.
For each pairing, they stated which was better on a 7-point Likert scale.
Specifically: "Which analogy is better?
The one on top or the one on the bottom?"
This item was kept minimal to eliminate any language that would bias responses to favor the mechanical base e.g., explicitly using the term "insight".
Each participant was randomly assigned 3 such pairings and 3 pairings of filler analogies (a block).
The study ended when they completed these and an attention check.
We fit a mixed-effects model with preference for mechanism as the outcome, a fixed intercept, and then a random intercept for participant id, psychology analogy, and physical-mechanical analogy.
This model showed a preference for the physical-mechanical analogies of roughly one point on the 7-point Likert (b = 1.09, 95% CI [0.65, 1.55], t(7.05) = 5.09, p = .001).
In fact, for every randomly-selected comparison tested in the study, the average selection favored the physical-mechanical direction (and most significantly so).
See Figure 1.
text.formatted: See Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1</ref>.

text.text: To ensure differences in length or word frequency were not driving our effects we performed a series of exploratory analyses.
First, we tested whether there were any differences on these variables between the analogies with psychological bases and those with physical mechanical bases.
The analogies with a psychological base were (insignificantly) shorter (t(9.05) = 1.89, p=.091) but used less common words (t(9.31) = 2.33, p = .044).
Given the slight difference in word frequency, we performed the main regression analysis again with length and frequency as covariates.
They had no significant relationship with preference (b = -.18, p = .309; b = .26, p = .151) and did not dilute the main effect (b = 1.076, 95% CI [0.72, 1.44], t(5.14) = 5.50, p =.003).
Participants consistently think the best analogies explaining the psychological in terms of the physical mechanical are better than those going in the opposite direction.
These findings were consistent across pairings and robust to controls.
It is possible however that the best physical mechanical to psychological analogies are especially goodbut overall the domains do not differ.
Moreover, the effects might be specific to the large language model we assigned to generate the stimuli.
We therefore conducted a more scoping survey of potential analogies in either direction in Study 2.
In this study, we wanted participants to compare a diverse sample of analogies.

Rather than just looking at the bestof-the-best, we sampled common physical mechanical and psychological phenomena, randomly paired them, and asked three popular large language models to create analogies in both directions out of the pairings.
For example, door handle and latch mechanism was paired with emotion regulation, and the LLM fashioned one analogy with door handle as the base and another with the emotion regulation as the base:

A door handle and latch mechanism is like emotion regulation: turning the handle changes the position of the latch so the door can open, much as regulating an emotion adjusts an internal response so a different action becomes possible.
Our predictions were the same as in Study 1.
Analogies generated with the physical mechanical stimulus as the base should be preferred to their mirror.
Study 2 was also a conservative test because many of the random pairings might not contain enough shared information across pairs to make any sort of reasonable analogy.

text.formatted: Code and stimuli are available at GitHub: <ref type="url" target="https://github.com/martxgr/analogies">https://github.com/martxgr/analogies</ref> Participants Power analyses on pilots suggested recruiting 100 participants per large language would give us over 80% power for detecting a effect.

text.text: Thus, we recruited 300 total participants on Prolific (50% female, 46% White, 36 years on average).
Participants who failed our preregistered attention check were excluded from the analysis (n = 3).
We followed a five-step procedure with the three leading LLMs (ChatGPT 5.6 Sol, Claude Opus 5, and Gemini Pro 3.1).
Each step involved using a separate chat, without memory.
(1) We generated the physical mechanical phenomena: "List 12 common physical-mechanical systems that most people know about and have a sense of how they work.
Output them to a one column csv."
(2) We generated the psychological phenomena: "List 12 common psychological systems that most people know about and have a sense of how they work.
Output them to a one column csv."
(3) We randomly selected 6 items from each set and then randomly paired every one of those six with a different item from the other set.
(4) We asked the LLM to elaborate analogies in one direction: "Here is a list of paired physical-mechanical and psychological systems.
For each row, please write a single sentence analogy of the form "x is like y: ..." where the psychological phenomenon is explained using the mechanical phenomenon.
The result should be 6 analogies."
(5) We asked the LLM to elaborate analogies in the opposite direction: "Here is a list of paired physical-mechanical and psychological systems.
For each row, please write a single sentence analogy of the form "x is like y: ..." where the physical-mechanical phenomenon is explained using the psychological phenomenon.
The result should be 6 analogies."
We generated a set of 12 filler analogies in the same way, except we substituted "biological" for every instance of physical-mechanical and "economic" for every instance of psychological.
All analogies are in the study materials on GitHub (https://github.com/martxgr/analogies).
text.formatted: All analogies are in the study materials on GitHub (<ref type="url" target="https://github.com/martxgr/analogies">https://github.com/martxgr/analogies</ref>).

text.text: After a brief introduction to the task (slightly varied from Study 1 to ensure robustness), participants were given 6 comparison trials and 6 filler trials.

On the comparison trials, an analogy explaining a physical mechanical phenomenon with a psychological phenomenon and an analogy explaining the same psychological phenomenon with the same physical mechanical phenomenon were provided.
Participants were simply asked which analogy was better on a 7-point Likert scale.
Filler trials were the same, except they used economic and biological phenomena.
The order of stimuli and trials was randomized.
After completing all 12 trials and an attention check, participants were thanked for their time and compensated.

For each large language model, we fit a mixed effects model, where a per-trial preference for physical mechanical base versus psychological base was predicted by a fixed intercept, with pairing and participant id as random intercepts.

For every model, participants showed a preference for analogies that explained the psychological in terms of the physical mechanical (GPT: β = 0.82, 95% CI [0.54, 1.11], t(12.12) = 5.93, p < .001; Claude: β = 0.95, 95% CI [0.71, 1.19], t(23.06) = 8.03, p < .001; Gemini: β = 1.11, 95% CI [0.85, 1.37], t(17.87) = 8.51, p < .001).
text.formatted: For every model, participants showed a preference for analogies that explained the psychological in terms of the physical mechanical (GPT: β = 0.82, 95% CI [0.54, 1.11], t(12.12) = 5.93, p < .001; Claude: β = 0.95, 95% CI [0.71, 1.19], t(23.06) = 8.03, p < .001; Gemini: β = 1.11, 95% CI [0.85, 1.37], t(17.87) = 8.51, p < .001).

text.text: Roughly, it translated to a point difference on a 7-point Likert scale.

We also fit a mixed effect model where a per-trial preference for a physical mechanical base over a psychological base was predicted by which large language model generated the stimuli (GPT, Claude, or Gemini), with participant id, pairing, and the interaction of pairing and large language model as random intercepts.
The overall effect was significant (β = 0.96, 95% CI [0.81, 1.12], t(17.60) = 12.86, p < .001); and did not differ between LLMs (F(2, 33.64) = 1.22, p = .307).
text.formatted: The overall effect was significant (β = 0.96, 95% CI [0.81, 1.12], t(17.60) = 12.86, p < .001); and did not differ between LLMs (F(2, 33.64) = 1.22, p = .307).

text.text: See Figure 2.
text.formatted: See Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_1">2</ref>.

text.text: As in Study 1, we performed exploratory control analyses for length and word frequency.

Unlike that Study, we found no differences between the analogy directions in the length (b = -1.78 words, 95% CI [-4.55, 1.00], t(5) = -1.65, p = .160) or frequency (b = 0.093, 95% CI [-0.036, 0.222], t(5) = 1.86, p = .121), even when controlling for the model that generated the stimuli.

Adding length and word frequency yielded null results for those variables (b = -0.070, 95% CI [-0.215, 0.074], t(12.98) = -1.05, p = .312; b = 0.018, 95% CI [-0.126, 0.163], t(12.98) = 0.28, p = .788, respectively) and did not meliorate the strength of the effect (b = 0.96, SE = 0.08, 95% CI [0.80, 1.13], t(14.3) = 12.66, p < .001).
text.formatted: Adding length and word frequency yielded null results for those variables (b = -0.070, 95% CI [-0.215, 0.074], t(12.98) = -1.05, p = .312; b = 0.018, 95% CI [-0.126, 0.163], t(12.98) = 0.28, p = .788, respectively) and did not meliorate the strength of the effect (b = 0.96, SE = 0.08, 95% CI [0.80, 1.13], t(14.3) = 12.66, p < .001).

text.text: As predicted, when given mirrored analogies of common physical mechanical and psychological phenomena, participants show a preference for the former as the base.

These effects persisted across all large language models we used to generate the stimuli and were not a consequence of more low-level differences between the analogies (length or use of frequent words).
Even though the base and target domains were randomly paired, a clear preference for mechanical bases was found.
Studies 1 and 2 suggest that people judge analogies that explain the psychological in terms of the physical mechanical as better than those going in the opposite direction.
But what happens when they generate the analogies themselves?
Are participants equally adept at explaining the physical mechanical in terms of the psychological as they are in the opposite direction, or do they show an asymmetry?
In addition, do they judge their own work in ways that align with the previous findings?
Since novel analogies tend to be difficult to create (Gentner et. al, 1993), this too is a conservative test.
text.formatted: Since novel analogies tend to be difficult to create <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(Gentner et. al, 1993)</ref>, this too is a conservative test.

text.formatted: Code and stimuli are available at GitHub: <ref type="url" target="https://github.com/martxgr/analogies">https://github.com/martxgr/analogies</ref> Participants Power analyses on pilots suggested recruiting 200 participants would give us over 80% power for detecting an effect.

text.text: Thus, we recruited 200 participants on Prolific (50% female, 46% White, 36 years on average).
Participants who failed our one preregistered attention check were excluded from the analysis (n = 3).
Participants were given a refresher of what an analogy is, and an example (the Bohr model of the atom).

Then they were given a list containing 5 physical mechanical phenomena (Bicycle, Clock, Washing machine, Elevator, Car Engine) and 5 psychological phenomena (Decision-making, Memory, Emotion regulation, Motivation, and Social Perception).
These were generated by ChatGPT 5.6 Sol when prompted (without memory) to share common and commonly understood phenomena from the respective domains.

Randomization was performed as follows: The phenomena of each domain were always presented with the other phenomena from that domain (i.e., all the mechanism phenomena remained with the other mechanism phenomena, and all the psychological with the other psychological).
However, which domain was at the beginning or end of the list was random (the mechanical could be first, or the psychological).
Then, within the domain, the phenomena were randomly ordered.
Participants first picked one phenomenon to explain (target).
Then, they picked something to explain with (base).
If they picked a psychological (or mechanical) phenomenon to explain, they would only have the mechanical (or psychological) phenomena to explain with.
Next, they were asked to generate an analogy in accordance with their selection.
If they wanted to change their mind, they could always go back and change their selection.
Finally, after generating their analogy, they rated how good or bad they thought it was on a 7-point Likert scale.
After selfreporting attention, they were thanked for their time and compensated.

After collecting these data, we asked ChatGPT 5.6 Sol to rate the vector of generated analogies like so: Please sort these responses into two categories: An analogy that explains a psychological phenomenon in terms of a physical mechanical phenomenon.
An analogy that explains a physical mechanical phenomenon in terms of a psychological phenomenon.
Output your categorization into a new column called "base," where the value for a response belonging to category 1 is 'mech' and for a response belonging to category 2 is 'psych.'"
First, there is the question of what participants chose to write.
We find no effect of using the physical mechanical stimuli as the base (exact binomial test, 95% CI [47.1, 61.4], p = .254).

We also find no statistically significant difference in the self-rated quality of these analogies (b = -0.28, 95% CI [-0.68, 0.12], t(194.1) = -1.37, p = .173) in a linear mixed effects model with mechanical item and psychological item as random intercepts.
Second, there is the question of what participants actually wrote.
As preregistered, we asked ChatGPT to rate whether the given analogy explained psychology in terms of mechanism or vice versa.
Using this metric, we found that most of the analogies were physical mechanical (147 of 197; exact binomial test, p < .001).
text.formatted: Using this metric, we found that most of the analogies were physical mechanical (147 of 197; exact binomial test, p < .001).

text.text: It seems that participants who had selected to use a psychological based "subverted" their own instructions at a rate of almost 46% (41 of 90), whereas those in the mechanical condition almost never did (1 of 107; Fisher's exact test, OR = 86.2, 95% CI [13.8, 3514.2], p < .001).
text.formatted: It seems that participants who had selected to use a psychological based "subverted" their own instructions at a rate of almost 46% (41 of 90), whereas those in the mechanical condition almost never did (1 of 107; Fisher's exact test, OR = 86.2, 95% CI [13.8, 3514.2], p < .001).

text.text: In an exploratory analysis, we compared the analogies with mechanical and psychological bases as determined by GPT on self-rated quality.
Now, the analogies with the mechanical base were given significantly higher ratings (b = -0.58, 95% CI [-1.03, -0.13], t(192.7) = -0.55, p = .011).
See Figure 3 for a compilation of the results.
text.formatted: See Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_2">3</ref> for a compilation of the results.

text.text: Participants more often created analogies with physical mechanical bases.
To our surprise, they did not assign themselves to do so.
But in the process of writing, they overwhelmingly ended up creating analogies in that direction.
When they did, they ended up rating their work more highly than those who did not.
The asymmetry between physical mechanical entities and psychological entities naturally leads to the question of whether the physical mechanical domain shows asymmetries with other broad classes.

We suggested in the introduction that the physical mechanical domain might be especially useful as base domains because so many of that domain's entities contain components with clear functions and mechanisms that recur in various combinations across many different kinds.
In addition, these components and their interactions often invoke spatial relations.

Spatial encoding of information may provide uniquely powerful support for cognition (e.g., Volpi & de Hevia, 2026; Yousif & Epstein, 2026), perhaps especially so for analogies and their relational architecture.
text.formatted: Spatial encoding of information may provide uniquely powerful support for cognition (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">Volpi & de Hevia, 2026;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">Yousif & Epstein, 2026)</ref>, perhaps especially so for analogies and their relational architecture.

text.text: This cognitive support may result in physical mechanical analogical bases yielding more informative analogies across several domains beyond psychology.
Study 4 asked whether the physical mechanical domain is a preferred base of analogical insights into other domains beyond psychology.

A systematic comparison to all possible domains at different levels is far beyond the scope of this paper; but a small handful of domains could increase the plausibility of a persistent analogical advantage.
We chose domains corresponding to large academic departments in universities where a core practice in those departments is to provide causal explanations: biology, chemistry, and economics.
We predicted that analogies with physical mechanical entities as bases would be preferred bases of analogies in comparison to those analogies where members of those three domains were bases.

text.text: We powered our study based on what was required to detect an effect in the previous studies.
Hence, we wanted 100 participant ratings of each comparison.
Given our design, this required the recruitment of 300 total participants on Prolific (50% female, 52% White, 37 years on average).
Participants who failed our preregistered attention check were excluded from the analysis (n = 7).
The design closely followed Study 2's.
Participants were given 6 comparison trials and 6 filler trials, where they were asked which analogy was better on a 7-point Likert scale.

This time, for the comparison trials, they received 2 trials comparing analogies using a biological and physical mechanical phenomenon; 2 comparing the chemical and physical mechanical; and 2 comparing the economic and physical mechanical.
Filler trials had them compare analogies with meteorology and astronomy bases/targets.
After completing all 12 trials (which were randomized), and an attention check, participants were thanked for their time and compensated.
We again closely followed Study 2's recipe.
We restricted ourselves to ChatGPT 5.6 Sol, without memory enabled.
(1) We generated the physical mechanical phenomena: "List 12 common physical-mechanical systems that most people know about and have a sense of how they work.
Output them to a one column csv."
(2) We generated the biological, chemical, and economic phenomena in the same way.
(3) We randomly selected 6 of each phenomena type, and randomly paired the same 6 physical mechanical phenomena with each of the others.
(4) As before, we asked the LLM to elaborate analogies in one direction and then the other: "Here is a list of paired physicalmechanical and {chemical, biological, or economic} phenomena.
For each row, please write a single sentence analogy of the form "x is like y: ..." where the {chemical, biological, or economic} phenomenon is explained using the mechanical phenomenon.
The result should be 6 analogies."
We generated a set of 12 filler analogies in the same way, except using astronomy and meteorology.
The non-filler analogies totaled 36: 6 physical mechanical phenomena paired with 6 chemical, 6 biological, and 6 economic stimuli, with two analogies produced from each pairing.
We only showed 6 of these analogies to each participant.

We used a Latin Square to ensure each participant viewed all 6 physical mechanical phenomena and two of each domain pairing, and that there was an even presentation of all 36 stimuli across participants.

As with Study 2, we fit a mixed effect model where a per-trial preference for physical mechanical base was predicted by which domain was contrasting (chemical, biological, or economic), with physical mechanical item, participant id, and the interaction of physical mechanical item and domain as random intercepts.
The overall effect was significant (β = 0.69, 95% CI [0.33, 1.04], t(5.41) = 4.90, p = .004); and did not differ between domains F(2, 9.49) = 2.36, p = .148).

If we run the same model, but filter for one comparison domain at a time (and remove the random intercept for the interaction of physical mechanical item and domain) we find a significant effect contrasting with the chemical (β = 0.51, 95% CI [0.20, 0.82], t(5.21) = 3.50, p = .016), biological (β = 0.67, 95% CI [0.17, 1.16], t(5.07) = 2.85, p = .035), and economic (β = 0.87, 95% CI [0.66, 1.09], t(6.40) = 8.60, p < .001) domains.
text.formatted: If we run the same model, but filter for one comparison domain at a time (and remove the random intercept for the interaction of physical mechanical item and domain) we find a significant effect contrasting with the chemical (β = 0.51, 95% CI [0.20, 0.82], t(5.21) = 3.50, p = .016), biological (β = 0.67, 95% CI [0.17, 1.16], t(5.07) = 2.85, p = .035), and economic (β = 0.87, 95% CI [0.66, 1.09], t(6.40) = 8.60, p < .001) domains.

text.text: There was no difference between analogies with the physical mechanical base in length and word frequency compared to the other domains (p's > 0.07) and as before, including length and frequency as covariates for the analogies did not change the significance of any effects.
text.formatted: There was no difference between analogies with the physical mechanical base in length and word frequency compared to the other domains (p's > 0.07) and as before, including length and frequency as covariates for the analogies did not change the significance of any effects.

text.text: See Figure 4.
text.formatted: See Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_3">4</ref>.

text.text: Mechanical bases had a consistent advantage over bases from the three new domains.
Thus, mechanics effects relative to psychology may have less to do with psychology lacking as a base, and more to do with mechanical entities excelling in that role.
These results may seem consistent with a reductionist view: domains lower in the reductionist hierarchy carry more explanatory power.
However, at least in this study, we found no significant difference between domains.
Analogical asymmetries exist not just between isolated cases, but also between entire domains.
People judge that mechanical entities can explain more about psychological entities than the reverse.

We observed this asymmetry when comparing the best analogies in either direction (Study 1), when we randomly paired bases and targets in either direction (Study 2), and when participants were asked to generate their own analogies (Study 3).
Our final study (Study 4) suggests a general preference for physical mechanical bases of analogical explanations relative to other domains.
All effects were remarkably consistent across participants and stimuli (50/51 pairings pointed toward a mechanical preference).
What makes the mechanical domain so fertile for explanations compared to the psychological?
It may be the causal graphs implied by mechanical systems (cf. Lee & Holyoak, 2008).
text.formatted: It may be the causal graphs implied by mechanical systems (cf. <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">Lee & Holyoak, 2008)</ref>.

text.text: For one, the mechanical domain's causal relations are deterministic.
A screw always goes deeper when tightened; an emotion regulation strategy does not always produce happiness.
Secondly, the mechanical domain's causal relations are (relatively) limited (cf. Norman, 1988).
text.formatted: Secondly, the mechanical domain's causal relations are (relatively) limited (cf. <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">Norman, 1988)</ref>.

text.text: Looking over the "common physical-mechanical" phenomena generated by the large language models, they are almost universally basic tools.

There is typically a straightforward path of causation, without any feedback loop or nesting of effects (e.g., for the door latch: pulling on the latch causes the latch to lift and releases the door).

In contrast, psychological phenomena tend to be multiply determined (e.g., a bad mood may emerge because of bad food, poor sleep, a tough conversation with a boss, with none of these factors being either necessary, nor sufficient).
Perhaps most deeply, the causal relations that constitute a given mechanical base are spatial (Hegarty & Sims, 1994; Hegarty, 2004).
text.formatted: Perhaps most deeply, the causal relations that constitute a given mechanical base are spatial <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">(Hegarty & Sims, 1994;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">Hegarty, 2004)</ref>.

text.text: Spatially representing relations may make them more durable in memory and easier to mentally manipulate).
Fleetingly few analogies with psychological bases can leverage these spatial qualities while almost all those with a mechanical base can.
The causal relations between the elements of the mechanical domain are thus simple, deterministic, and spatial.
This may grant the domain a substantial explanatory edge over the psychological -and perhaps other domains, as well.
Psychological phenomena may serve as launchpads for other sorts of conceptual growth.

In particular, psychological phenomena may be more effective when the objective is not to explain a causal relation -as with an analogy -but instead to confer properties onto an entity -as with many metaphors (Keil, 1986; Lehrer, 1978).
text.formatted: In particular, psychological phenomena may be more effective when the objective is not to explain a causal relation -as with an analogy -but instead to confer properties onto an entity -as with many metaphors <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">(Keil, 1986;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">Lehrer, 1978)</ref>.

text.text: For example, we commonly ascribe emotional states to artifacts, "the car complained on its way up the hill", or anthropomorphizing when describing a teleological system, "the liver hates alcohol".
None of these examples illuminate how a system works.
But they do characterize a system's state through reference to another, more familiar one (psychology).
The method of comparing domains of analogies -rather than individual analogies -promises to contribute to the cognitive science of explanation (cf. Lombrozo, 2026; Vagnino & Walker, 2026).
text.formatted: The method of comparing domains of analogies -rather than individual analogies -promises to contribute to the cognitive science of explanation (cf. <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">Lombrozo, 2026;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">Vagnino & Walker, 2026)</ref>.

text.text: Suppose for a moment, as these results suggest, that the physical mechanical domain is the best launchpad for explanation.
This opens a space in which to explore what makes for a good explanation: to understand what is special the mechanical domain is in part to understand properties of an effective explanation.

It also opens a space to explore the development of explanations: how does the physical mechanical domain inform the generation of explanations throughout development, from when it overlaps with one of few core domains in early development, to when it is just one among many?
Finally, there are normative implications.

If the physical mechanical domain is best for explanation, it may (1) be beneficial to prioritize learning about mechanical systems, especially earlier in development, and (2) use that mechanical knowledge for learning in other domains more often (cf. Clement, 1993).
text.formatted: If the physical mechanical domain is best for explanation, it may (1) be beneficial to prioritize learning about mechanical systems, especially earlier in development, and (2) use that mechanical knowledge for learning in other domains more often (cf. <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">Clement, 1993)</ref>.

text.text: Future research might test the mechanical domain against further domains and pursue these questions.
We acknowledge several limitations to this work.
First, our hypotheses were only tested within-subject; we had participants compare analogies side-by-side.
Without proper anchoring, a between-subjects design is unlikely to show a similar effect.
Second, we relied on large language models for the generation of our stimuli.
This conferred several advantages: (1) the same procedure can be used by scientists looking to replicate our findings, and (2) the stimuli themselves are free of experimenter biases.
Moreover, Study 3 suggests that participants would be unreliable sources of analogies.
However, large language models have biases of their own.
For instance, they may lack internal models (or at least internal models that remotely resemble those of human cognition; cf. Vafa et al, 2024).
text.formatted: For instance, they may lack internal models (or at least internal models that remotely resemble those of human cognition; cf. <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">Vafa et al, 2024)</ref>.

text.text: This could inhibit analogy generation.
Future research might sample vast language repositories (like Reddit) for persongenerated analogies.
Finally, our participants were recruited largely from wealthy, English speaking nations.
Which psychological and mechanical systems would exemplify their respective domains might differ in other cultures, and in turn rebalance the asymmetry.
We also caution that the explanatory boosts from physical mechanical bases may not always be a benefit.
One must always be vigilant as to whether such bases suggest more than they should, such as excessively deterministic models of the target.
In short, these studies show that analogical symmetries exist not just between isolated pairs but between entire, large-scale domains.
In particular, we find that the mechanical domain is a more fertile ground for explaining phenomena than the psychological.
This advantage extends to three other domains, as well.
This raises further questions about the explanatory advantage and how best to exploit it.
